question_html: Under section 2(42) of the Companies Act, 2013, what two cumulative conditions must a company or body corporate incorporated outside India satisfy to be classified as a 'foreign company'?

options.A: It must (a) have a place of business in India, whether by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, AND (b) conduct any business activity in India in any other manner
options.B: It must merely be incorporated outside India, with no further requirement of having a place of business or conducting business activity in India at all
options.C: It must either have a place of business in India OR conduct business activity in India, with the two conditions being alternative rather than cumulative
options.D: It must have its registered office physically situated within India while remaining incorporated abroad, since 'foreign company' under section 2(42) refers only to physical (never electronic) places of business

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) It must (a) have a place of business in India, whether by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, AND (b) conduct any business activity in India in any other manner

Section 2(42) is a two-limb, cumulative definition - mere incorporation outside India does not by itself make a company a 'foreign company'; it must additionally have a place of business in India (physically, through an agent, or electronically) and conduct business activity in India in some manner.

question_html: Under Rule 2(1)(h) of the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014, 'electronic mode' is defined broadly to include which categories of activity, and what specific carve-out applies to International Financial Services Centres (IFSCs)?

options.A: 'Electronic mode' is confined strictly to e-mail-based communication between the foreign company and its Indian customers; telemedicine, cloud computing, and social-media-based activities fall entirely outside its scope
options.B: 'Electronic mode' broadly includes business-to-business and business-to-consumer transactions, data interchange and digital supply transactions; offering/accepting deposits or subscriptions in securities in India or from Indian citizens; financial settlements, web-based marketing, advisory/transactional/database services and supply chain management; online services such as telemarketing, telecommuting, telemedicine, and education/information research; and all related data communication services (by e-mail, mobile devices, social media, cloud computing, etc.) - however, electronic-based offering, subscription, or listing of securities in IFSCs set up under section 18 of the SEZ Act, 2005 is expressly NOT construed as 'electronic mode' for section 2(42) purposes
options.C: There is no IFSC carve-out under Rule 2(1)(h); electronic-based offering, subscription, or listing of securities in an IFSC is treated identically to any other electronic-mode activity for section 2(42) purposes
options.D: 'Electronic mode' applies only where the company's main server is physically installed within India; activities routed through servers located outside India are excluded from the definition entirely

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) 'Electronic mode' broadly includes business-to-business and business-to-consumer transactions, data interchange and digital supply transactions; offering/accepting deposits or subscriptions in securities in India or from Indian citizens; financial settlements, web-based marketing, advisory/transactional/database services and supply chain management; online services such as telemarketing, telecommuting, telemedicine, and education/information research; and all related data communication services (by e-mail, mobile devices, social media, cloud computing, etc.) - however, electronic-based offering, subscription, or listing of securities in IFSCs set up under section 18 of the SEZ Act, 2005 is expressly NOT construed as 'electronic mode' for section 2(42) purposes

The Rules deliberately give 'electronic mode' an expansive, illustrative (not exhaustive) scope covering a wide range of digital business activities regardless of where the main server is installed, while carving out one narrow exception - electronic-based securities offering/subscription/listing within IFSCs - which is not treated as 'electronic mode' for classifying a company as a foreign company under section 2(42).

question_html: Zakpak Ltd., a shipping company incorporated in Japan, sets up a branch office in India after obtaining necessary RBI approvals. Is this branch office treated as a 'place of business' for the purpose of the foreign company provisions?

options.A: No - a branch office is treated as a wholly separate legal entity from its foreign parent and therefore does not, by itself, constitute a 'place of business' of the parent company under Chapter XXII
options.B: No - only a full subsidiary company incorporated in India (never a branch office) can be treated as a 'place of business' of a foreign parent for purposes of Chapter XXII
options.C: Yes - branch offices are generally considered a reflection of the parent company's office; thus, branch offices of a company incorporated outside India are treated as a place of business for conducting business activity in India, and Zakpak Ltd. must comply with the provisions of Chapter XXII and other applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: Whether a branch office counts as a 'place of business' depends solely on whether it independently earns a profit; a loss-making branch office is excluded from the definition regardless of its business activities

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - branch offices are generally considered a reflection of the parent company's office; thus, branch offices of a company incorporated outside India are treated as a place of business for conducting business activity in India, and Zakpak Ltd. must comply with the provisions of Chapter XXII and other applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013

The study material treats a branch office as a reflection of the parent company's office - it is squarely a 'place of business' in India, bringing the foreign company within the scope of Chapter XXII and other applicable Companies Act provisions concerning its Indian business activity.

question_html: Under section 379(1), which provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 apply to EVERY foreign company (as defined in section 2(42)), without any additional shareholding-based condition?

options.A: Only section 380 (documents to Registrar) applies to all foreign companies; sections 381 to 393 apply only where a majority of the foreign company's shareholding is Indian-held
options.B: Sections 379 to 393A apply to all foreign companies only if they have established a physical (not electronic) place of business in India, with purely electronic-mode foreign companies being entirely outside the Act's scope
options.C: No provision of Chapter XXII applies to a foreign company unless and until it is separately incorporated as a subsidiary company under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: Sections 380 to 386 (both inclusive) and sections 392 and 393 apply to all foreign companies falling within the section 2(42) definition, with no additional condition regarding Indian shareholding

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Sections 380 to 386 (both inclusive) and sections 392 and 393 apply to all foreign companies falling within the section 2(42) definition, with no additional condition regarding Indian shareholding

Section 379(1) casts a wide net: sections 380-386 and sections 392-393 apply to every company meeting the section 2(42) definition of 'foreign company', regardless of its shareholding pattern - the more stringent 'as if an Indian company' compliance under section 379(2) is a separate, additional layer triggered only by the 50% Indian-holding threshold.

question_html: Under section 379(2), what shareholding threshold, held by which categories of persons, triggers the requirement that a foreign company comply with Chapter XXII and other prescribed provisions 'as if it were a company incorporated in India', and how may that threshold be met?

options.A: Where not less than 50% of the paid-up share capital (whether equity, preference, or partly equity and partly preference) of a foreign company is held by (i) one or more citizens of India, or (ii) one or more companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India, or (iii) a combination of both - whether singly or in the aggregate - the foreign company must also comply with Chapter XXII and such other prescribed provisions of the Act with regard to its business carried on in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India
options.B: The threshold is 100% (i.e., wholly Indian-owned) paid-up equity share capital held exclusively by companies incorporated in India; holdings by individual Indian citizens or by preference shareholders are disregarded entirely for this computation
options.C: The threshold is 26% of paid-up share capital, matching the general 'significant beneficial ownership' threshold used elsewhere in the Companies Act, 2013, rather than 50%
options.D: The threshold applies only to holdings by Indian citizens; holdings by Indian companies or bodies corporate are excluded from the computation, however large, under section 379(2)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Where not less than 50% of the paid-up share capital (whether equity, preference, or partly equity and partly preference) of a foreign company is held by (i) one or more citizens of India, or (ii) one or more companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India, or (iii) a combination of both - whether singly or in the aggregate - the foreign company must also comply with Chapter XXII and such other prescribed provisions of the Act with regard to its business carried on in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India

Section 379(2) sets a 50% (not less than) threshold on paid-up share capital, aggregating holdings across Indian citizens and Indian companies/bodies corporate (singly or combined, and across equity and preference capital), and once crossed, subjects the foreign company to Chapter XXII and other prescribed provisions in relation to its Indian business as though it were itself an Indian-incorporated company.

question_html: Emaar Company LLC, incorporated in Dubai with a place of business in India, has the following shareholding: Hinduja Company Limited (an Indian company) holds 26%, Vaishali Company Limited (an Indian company) holds 25%, and citizens of Dubai hold the remaining balance. Does section 379(2) apply to Emaar Company LLC?

options.A: No - since neither Hinduja Company Limited nor Vaishali Company Limited individually holds 50% or more, their holdings cannot be aggregated, and section 379(2) is therefore inapplicable to Emaar Company LLC
options.B: Yes - the aggregate holding of the two Indian companies (26% + 25% = 51%) exceeds the 50% threshold, so Emaar Company LLC must also comply with the provisions of Chapter XXII and such other prescribed provisions of the Act with regard to the business carried on by its place of business in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India
options.C: No - section 379(2) applies only where the entire paid-up share capital (100%) is held by Indian citizens or Indian companies; a 51% aggregate holding falls short of this requirement
options.D: The applicability of section 379(2) cannot be determined without knowing whether Emaar Company LLC's shares are equity or preference shares, since only equity holdings count toward the 50% threshold

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - the aggregate holding of the two Indian companies (26% + 25% = 51%) exceeds the 50% threshold, so Emaar Company LLC must also comply with the provisions of Chapter XXII and such other prescribed provisions of the Act with regard to the business carried on by its place of business in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India

Section 379(2) expressly permits aggregation - holdings by multiple Indian companies/citizens, whether singly or in the aggregate, count toward the 50% threshold; here, Hinduja Company Limited's 26% plus Vaishali Company Limited's 25% aggregate to 51%, comfortably crossing the threshold and triggering section 379(2)'s enhanced compliance requirement.

question_html: What additional supporting document must accompany a foreign company's Form FC-1 application under the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014, in relation to regulatory approvals for establishing a place of business in India?

options.A: The application must be supported with an attested copy of approval from the Reserve Bank of India under the Foreign Exchange Management Act or Regulations (and from other regulators, if any, whose approval is required to establish a place of business), or, alternatively, a declaration from the authorised representative that no such approval is required

question_html: If a foreign company ceases to have a place of business in India, what must it do, and what is the effect on its obligation to deliver documents to the Registrar?

options.A: The company must apply to the Central Government for formal dissolution of its Indian registration; simply notifying the Registrar of cessation is insufficient, and filing obligations continue indefinitely until such dissolution is granted

options.A: The default financial year is the calendar year (1st January to 31st December) for every foreign company, with no provision anywhere permitting deviation from this calendar-year default for consolidation purposes
options.B: 'Financial year' means the period ending on 31st March every year (or, where incorporated on or after 1st January of a year, the period ending on 31st March of the following year); however, where the company/body corporate is a holding, subsidiary, or associate company of a company incorporated outside India and is required to follow a different financial year for consolidation of accounts outside India, the Central Government may, on application in the prescribed form and manner, allow any period as its financial year, whether or not that period is a year

question_html: Under section 382, what must every foreign company conspicuously exhibit outside its offices in India, and what must it state on its business letters, bill-heads, and other official publications?

options.A: Section 382 requires display of the name and country of incorporation only in the local language, with English-character display being optional at the foreign company's discretion
options.B: Section 382 requires exhibition of the name and country of incorporation only on official publications distributed outside India; no exhibition requirement applies to offices or places of business physically situated within India
options.C: It must conspicuously exhibit, on the outside of every office or place where it carries on business in India, the name of the company and the country of incorporation, in legible English characters and also in the local language(s) in general use in that locality; it must also cause the name of the company and country of incorporation to be stated in legible English characters on all business letters, bill-heads, letter paper, notices, and other official publications
options.D: Section 382 requires only the company's registration number (not its name or country of incorporation) to be exhibited outside its Indian offices and stated on business correspondence

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) It must conspicuously exhibit, on the outside of every office or place where it carries on business in India, the name of the company and the country of incorporation, in legible English characters and also in the local language(s) in general use in that locality; it must also cause the name of the company and country of incorporation to be stated in legible English characters on all business letters, bill-heads, letter paper, notices, and other official publications

Section 382 imposes a dual-language exhibition requirement (English plus the local language(s) of the office's locality) outside every Indian place of business, and a consistent English-character disclosure of name and country of incorporation across business letters, bill-heads, notices, and official publications - promoting transparency about the entity's foreign origin.

question_html: If the liability of the members of a foreign company is limited, what additional notice must the company give, and where must this notice appear?

options.A: No additional notice is required beyond the ordinary name and country-of-incorporation disclosures under section 382(a) and (b); the limited-liability status of members is a private matter requiring no separate public disclosure
options.B: The additional notice of limited liability need be given only once, at the time of the foreign company's initial FC-1 registration, and need not thereafter appear on any ongoing business correspondence or office signage
options.C: The additional notice of limited liability must be published as a newspaper advertisement in at least two Indian newspapers annually, rather than being displayed on correspondence or office premises
options.D: The company must cause notice of the limited-liability fact to be stated, in legible English characters, in every prospectus issued and in all business letters, bill-heads, letter paper, notices, advertisements, and other official publications; it must also be conspicuously exhibited outside every Indian office or place of business, in legible English characters and in the local language(s) of that locality

question_html: Under section 383, when is any process, notice, or other document required to be served on a foreign company deemed to be sufficiently served?

options.A: Service is deemed sufficient if it is addressed to any person whose name and address have been delivered to the Registrar under section 380, and is left at, or sent by post to, that delivered address, or served by electronic mode
options.B: Service is deemed sufficient only if personally handed to a director of the foreign company at the foreign company's registered office located outside India, regardless of any Indian address delivered to the Registrar
options.C: Service is deemed sufficient only if published as a public notice in the Official Gazette of India, with no provision for service by post, electronic mode, or delivery to a section 380-notified person
options.D: Section 383 provides no deeming provision at all for service on a foreign company; every service must be proved through actual, demonstrated receipt by a director of the company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Service is deemed sufficient if it is addressed to any person whose name and address have been delivered to the Registrar under section 380, and is left at, or sent by post to, that delivered address, or served by electronic mode

question_html: Under section 384, does section 71 (issue of debentures) apply to a foreign company, and within what period must a foreign company file its annual return (Form FC-4) with the Registrar?

options.A: Section 71 does not apply to foreign companies at all, since debenture issuance is treated as exclusively governed by the foreign company's home-country law; the annual return must be filed within 180 days of the close of the financial year
options.B: Yes - the provisions of section 71 (issue of debentures) apply mutatis mutandis to a foreign company; separately, every foreign company shall prepare and file an annual return in Form FC-4, along with prescribed fees, within a period of 60 days from the last day of its financial year, containing particulars as they stood on the close of the financial year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - the provisions of section 71 (issue of debentures) apply mutatis mutandis to a foreign company; separately, every foreign company shall prepare and file an annual return in Form FC-4, along with prescribed fees, within a period of 60 days from the last day of its financial year, containing particulars as they stood on the close of the financial year

Section 384 extends section 71's debenture provisions to foreign companies mutatis mutandis, and separately (per the Rules) requires the Form FC-4 annual return to be filed within 60 days from the last day of the financial year - a distinctly shorter window than the 6-month timeline applicable to financial statements under section 381.

question_html: To what extent does section 128 (books of account) apply to a foreign company, and under what circumstance is a foreign company required to comply with section 135 (Corporate Social Responsibility)?

options.A: Section 128 applies to a foreign company in full, requiring it to maintain books of account covering its ENTIRE global operations (not merely its Indian business) at its principal place of business in India
options.B: A foreign company is categorically and permanently exempt from CSR obligations under section 135, regardless of the scale of its Indian business operations or whether it independently meets the section 135(1) thresholds
options.C: Section 128 applies to a foreign company to the extent of requiring it to keep, at its principal place of business in India, books of account with respect to monies received and spent, sales and purchases made, and assets and liabilities, in the course of or in relation to its business in India; separately, under Rule 3 of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014, a foreign company that fulfils the criteria specified under section 135(1) is required to comply with section 135, subject to such exceptions, modifications, and adaptations as may be prescribed by rules
options.D: Books of account under section 128 need be kept only at the foreign company's registered office outside India; no Indian-located books of account are required under section 384

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Section 128 applies to a foreign company to the extent of requiring it to keep, at its principal place of business in India, books of account with respect to monies received and spent, sales and purchases made, and assets and liabilities, in the course of or in relation to its business in India; separately, under Rule 3 of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014, a foreign company that fulfils the criteria specified under section 135(1) is required to comply with section 135, subject to such exceptions, modifications, and adaptations as may be prescribed by rules

Section 384 tailors section 128's books-of-account requirement to the foreign company's Indian business specifically (monies received/spent, sales/purchases, assets/liabilities relating to Indian operations, kept at the Indian principal place of business), and separately makes CSR obligations under section 135 applicable to a foreign company that independently meets the section 135(1) thresholds, subject to prescribed exceptions and modifications.

question_html: Do the provisions of Chapter VI (Registration of Charges) apply to charges on properties created or acquired by a foreign company?

options.A: 'Director' is defined identically to section 2(34) of the Act with no extension for shadow-director-like persons, and 'place of business' is confined strictly to a company's registered office, expressly excluding any share transfer or registration office
options.B: 'Certified' means certified in the prescribed manner to be a true copy or a correct translation; 'director', in relation to a foreign company, includes any person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the Board of Directors of the company is accustomed to act; and 'place of business' includes a share transfer or registration office

question_html: Indian citizens incorporate a company in Singapore for the purpose of carrying on business exclusively in Singapore, with no place of business or business activity of any kind in India. Is this company a 'foreign company' under the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Yes - since Indian citizens incorporated the company, it automatically qualifies as a 'foreign company' under section 2(42), regardless of whether it has any place of business or conducts any business activity in India
options.B: Yes - any company incorporated outside India, by anyone, is automatically a 'foreign company' under the Companies Act, 2013, without any requirement of an Indian place of business or business activity
options.C: No - despite being incorporated outside India by Indian citizens, the company does not fall within the definition of a 'foreign company' because it has no place of business in India and conducts no business activity in India; incorporation abroad by Indian citizens is immaterial - what matters is whether the company has a place of business in India and conducts business activity there
options.D: The company's status depends entirely on the percentage of Indian citizens among its shareholders; since this is unspecified, its status as a foreign company cannot be determined

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - despite being incorporated outside India by Indian citizens, the company does not fall within the definition of a 'foreign company' because it has no place of business in India and conducts no business activity in India; incorporation abroad by Indian citizens is immaterial - what matters is whether the company has a place of business in India and conducts business activity there

The study material's own illustration confirms this: a company incorporated in Singapore by Indian citizens, but with no place of business or business activity in India, does NOT fall within the section 2(42) definition of 'foreign company' - the identity of the incorporators is immaterial; what matters is the presence of a place of business and business activity within India.

question_html: Under section 387(1), before a prospectus offering securities of a company incorporated (or to be incorporated) outside India may be issued, circulated, or distributed in India, what must the prospectus be, and what particulars must it generally contain?

options.A: The prospectus need only be dated (signing is optional), and no particulars regarding the company's constitutional documents, place/date of incorporation, or place of business in India are required under section 387(1)
options.B: The prospectus must be signed but need not be dated, and it need only comply with section 26 matters, with no additional particulars regarding constitution, incorporation, or Indian inspection address required
options.C: Section 387(1) applies only where the company has already established a place of business in India; prospectuses of companies that have not yet established such a place of business are entirely outside its scope
options.D: No person shall issue, circulate, or distribute in India any such prospectus unless it is dated and signed, and contains particulars regarding: the instrument constituting/defining the company's constitution; the enactments/provisions under which incorporation was effected; the Indian address where such instruments/enactments (or certified English translations) can be inspected; the date and country of incorporation; and whether the company has established a place of business in India (and if so, its principal office address) - in addition to stating the matters specified under section 26

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No person shall issue, circulate, or distribute in India any such prospectus unless it is dated and signed, and contains particulars regarding: the instrument constituting/defining the company's constitution; the enactments/provisions under which incorporation was effected; the Indian address where such instruments/enactments (or certified English translations) can be inspected; the date and country of incorporation; and whether the company has established a place of business in India (and if so, its principal office address) - in addition to stating the matters specified under section 26

question_html: Under the proviso to section 387(1), which particulars are exempted, and under what timing condition does this exemption apply?

options.A: The particulars relating to (1) the instrument constituting/defining the company's constitution, (2) the enactments/provisions under which incorporation was effected, and (3) the Indian inspection address for those instruments/enactments, need NOT be included where the prospectus is issued more than 2 years after the date at which the company is entitled to commence business
options.B: The exemption covers all five categories of particulars listed under section 387(1)(a), including the date/country of incorporation and the place-of-business disclosure, once 2 years have elapsed since the company was entitled to commence business
options.C: The exemption applies where the prospectus is issued LESS than (not more than) 2 years after the company became entitled to commence business, reversing the actual statutory timing condition
options.D: There is no such exemption under section 387; every prospectus, regardless of how long after incorporation it is issued, must contain all five categories of particulars specified in section 387(1)(a) without exception

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The particulars relating to (1) the instrument constituting/defining the company's constitution, (2) the enactments/provisions under which incorporation was effected, and (3) the Indian inspection address for those instruments/enactments, need NOT be included where the prospectus is issued more than 2 years after the date at which the company is entitled to commence business

The proviso to section 387(1) exempts only the first three (of five) particular categories - constitutional instrument, enabling enactments, and Indian inspection address - and only where the prospectus is issued MORE than 2 years after the company became entitled to commence business, as illustrated by the Mir Company LLC example in the study material.

question_html: Under section 387(2), is a condition requiring an applicant for securities to waive compliance with the section 387(1) requirements, or to be deemed to have notice of matters not specifically referred to in the prospectus, enforceable?

options.A: Yes - such a waiver condition is fully enforceable provided the applicant expressly consents to it in writing at the time of subscribing for the securities
options.B: No - any such condition, requiring or binding an applicant to waive compliance with section 387(1) requirements, or purporting to impute him with notice of any contract, document, or matter not specifically referred to in the prospectus, shall be VOID; section 387(2) provides no exception permitting non-compliance with section 387(1) by anyone responsible for issuing or circulating the prospectus
options.C: Such a waiver condition is enforceable only in respect of institutional (not retail) applicants for securities, since section 387(2) distinguishes between categories of investors
options.D: Section 387(2) permits such waivers so long as the issuing company separately obtains Central Government approval before including the waiver clause in the prospectus

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - any such condition, requiring or binding an applicant to waive compliance with section 387(1) requirements, or purporting to impute him with notice of any contract, document, or matter not specifically referred to in the prospectus, shall be VOID; section 387(2) provides no exception permitting non-compliance with section 387(1) by anyone responsible for issuing or circulating the prospectus

Section 387(2) is an anti-avoidance provision - it renders void any contractual attempt to make applicants waive their entitlement to section 387(1) compliance or to be deemed to have constructive notice of matters outside the prospectus, and creates no exception for the party responsible for the prospectus to escape section 387(1)'s substantive requirements.

question_html: Where a prospectus (of a company incorporated or to be incorporated outside India) includes a statement purporting to be made by an expert, what condition under section 388 must be satisfied before such a prospectus may be issued, circulated, or distributed in India?

options.A: An expert's ORAL consent, communicated informally to any officer of the issuing company, is sufficient; no written consent or statement in the prospectus regarding such consent is required under section 388
options.B: Section 388 requires the expert's consent only where the prospectus is being issued for the first time; consent is not required for any subsequent re-issue of a substantially similar prospectus
options.C: The expert must have given, and must not have withdrawn before delivery of the prospectus for registration, his written consent to the issue of the prospectus with the statement included in the form and context in which it appears; alternatively, there must appear in the prospectus a statement that he has given and has not withdrawn such consent - failing either, the prospectus cannot lawfully be issued, circulated, or distributed in India
options.D: Section 388 requires consent from the company's own directors (not from the expert whose statement is included) before a prospectus containing an expert's statement may be issued

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The expert must have given, and must not have withdrawn before delivery of the prospectus for registration, his written consent to the issue of the prospectus with the statement included in the form and context in which it appears; alternatively, there must appear in the prospectus a statement that he has given and has not withdrawn such consent - failing either, the prospectus cannot lawfully be issued, circulated, or distributed in India

Section 388 makes an expert's written, unwithdrawn consent (given before delivery of the prospectus for registration) a precondition for lawfully issuing a prospectus containing that expert's statement - a safeguard ensuring experts cannot be quoted in Indian securities offerings without their informed agreement.

question_html: Under section 388(1)(b), what additional effect must the prospectus have where an application for securities is made pursuant to it?

options.A: The prospectus must have the effect of rendering all persons concerned bound exclusively by the foreign company's home-country securities law, to the express exclusion of sections 33 and 40 of the Companies Act, 2013

question_html: Under section 389, before a prospectus offering subscription in securities of a company incorporated (or to be incorporated) outside India may be issued in India, what three things must be true of the copy delivered for registration to the Registrar?

options.A: A copy of the prospectus, certified by the chairperson of the company and two other directors as having been approved by resolution of the managing body, must have been delivered for registration to the Registrar; the prospectus must state on its face that a copy has been so delivered; and there must be endorsed on, or attached to, the copy, any consent to the issue required by section 388 and such documents as may be prescribed
options.B: The copy need be certified only by a single director (any director, not specifically the chairperson plus two others), and no statement on the face of the prospectus regarding delivery for registration is required
options.C: The copy must be certified by the company's statutory auditor (not by the chairperson and directors), and no endorsement of section 388 consents or prescribed documents is required to be attached
options.D: Registration under section 389 is optional; a foreign company may choose either to register its prospectus with the Registrar or to proceed directly with issuance without registration, at its discretion

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) A copy of the prospectus, certified by the chairperson of the company and two other directors as having been approved by resolution of the managing body, must have been delivered for registration to the Registrar; the prospectus must state on its face that a copy has been so delivered; and there must be endorsed on, or attached to, the copy, any consent to the issue required by section 388 and such documents as may be prescribed

Section 389 imposes three cumulative pre-issuance conditions - director-certification (chairperson plus two other directors, evidencing Board/managing-body approval) of the Registrar-delivered copy, an on-face statement confirming delivery for registration, and endorsement/attachment of section 388 consents and other prescribed documents (such as expert consents, managing director/manager appointment contracts, material contracts from the preceding 2 years, underwriting agreements, and powers of attorney).

question_html: What does 'Indian Depository Receipts' (IDR) mean under the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014, and over which four matters may the Central Government make rules under section 390?

options.A: IDR means a depository receipt created by a foreign depository outside India and authorised by an Indian company - i.e., the reverse structure of the actual definition, which instead involves a Domestic Depository in India and a foreign issuing company
options.B: IDR means any instrument in the form of a depository receipt created by a Domestic Depository in India and authorised by a company incorporated outside India making an issue of such depository receipts; the Central Government may make rules for: (i) the offer of IDRs; (ii) disclosure requirements in the prospectus/letter of offer issued in connection with IDRs; (iii) the manner in which IDRs shall be dealt with in depository mode and by custodians/underwriters; and (iv) the manner of sale, transfer, or transmission of IDRs by a company incorporated (or to be incorporated) outside India, whether or not it has established a place of business in India
options.C: The Central Government's rule-making power under section 390 is confined solely to setting the minimum issue size for IDRs, with disclosure requirements, depository-mode dealing, and transfer/transmission matters left entirely to SEBI
options.D: IDRs may be issued only by a foreign company that has already established a physical place of business in India; section 390 and Rule 13 make no provision for IDR issuance by a company with no established Indian place of business

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) IDR means any instrument in the form of a depository receipt created by a Domestic Depository in India and authorised by a company incorporated outside India making an issue of such depository receipts; the Central Government may make rules for: (i) the offer of IDRs; (ii) disclosure requirements in the prospectus/letter of offer issued in connection with IDRs; (iii) the manner in which IDRs shall be dealt with in depository mode and by custodians/underwriters; and (iv) the manner of sale, transfer, or transmission of IDRs by a company incorporated (or to be incorporated) outside India, whether or not it has established a place of business in India

An IDR is created by an Indian Domestic Depository but authorised by the foreign issuing company - and, notably, Rule 13 permits IDR issuance whether or not the foreign company has established (or will establish) any place of business in India; section 390 empowers the Central Government to make rules spanning the offer, prospectus disclosure, depository-mode dealing, and sale/transfer/transmission of such IDRs.

question_html: Under section 234(2), may a foreign company merge into a company registered under the Companies Act, 2013 (or vice versa), and if so, subject to what prior approval, and in what forms may consideration be paid to the shareholders of the merging company?

options.A: A foreign company may merge into an Indian company only with the prior approval of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and consideration to shareholders may be paid ONLY in cash - Depository Receipts are not a permissible form of consideration under section 234(2)
options.B: Section 234(2) prohibits any merger of a foreign company into an Indian company under any circumstance; only mergers between two Indian-incorporated companies are permitted under Chapter XV
options.C: Yes - subject to the provisions of any other law for the time being in force, a foreign company may, WITH THE PRIOR APPROVAL of the Reserve Bank of India, merge into a company registered under the Companies Act, 2013, or vice versa; the terms and conditions of the scheme may provide for payment of consideration to the shareholders of the merging company in cash, or in Depository Receipts, or partly in cash and partly in Depository Receipts, as per the scheme drawn up for the purpose
options.D: Prior approval of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) alone suffices for such cross-border mergers; no separate approval of the Reserve Bank of India is required under section 234(2)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - subject to the provisions of any other law for the time being in force, a foreign company may, WITH THE PRIOR APPROVAL of the Reserve Bank of India, merge into a company registered under the Companies Act, 2013, or vice versa; the terms and conditions of the scheme may provide for payment of consideration to the shareholders of the merging company in cash, or in Depository Receipts, or partly in cash and partly in Depository Receipts, as per the scheme drawn up for the purpose

Section 234(2) permits cross-border mergers (foreign-into-Indian or Indian-into-foreign) with the Reserve Bank of India's prior approval, offering flexibility in consideration structuring - cash, Depository Receipts, or a combination of both - as drawn up in the merger scheme, subject to any other applicable law.

question_html: For the specific purposes of section 234(2) (merger/amalgamation with a foreign company), how does the Explanation to that sub-section define 'foreign company', and how does this differ from the general section 2(42) definition used elsewhere in Chapter XXII?

options.A: The Explanation to section 234(2) uses the identical section 2(42) definition, with no broadening or narrowing of scope for merger purposes specifically
options.B: The Explanation to section 234(2) NARROWS the definition relative to section 2(42), requiring not only a place of business in India but also that at least 50% of the foreign company's shares be Indian-held before it can participate in a merger
options.C: The Explanation to section 234(2) confines 'foreign company' to companies incorporated in jurisdictions with which India has a bilateral investment treaty, a qualification absent from the general section 2(42) definition
options.D: For section 234(2) purposes, 'foreign company' means any company or body corporate incorporated outside India, WHETHER OR NOT it has a place of business in India - a broader meaning than section 2(42), which additionally requires the company to have a place of business in India and conduct business activity there

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) For section 234(2) purposes, 'foreign company' means any company or body corporate incorporated outside India, WHETHER OR NOT it has a place of business in India - a broader meaning than section 2(42), which additionally requires the company to have a place of business in India and conduct business activity there

Unlike the general section 2(42) definition (which requires both an Indian place of business and Indian business activity), the Explanation to section 234(2) deliberately widens 'foreign company' for merger purposes to cover any company or body corporate incorporated outside India regardless of whether it has any place of business in India - facilitating cross-border mergers even with foreign entities that have no Indian presence at all.

question_html: Under section 391(1), the provisions of sections 34 to 36 apply to which two categories of issuance, and what does each of sections 34, 35, and 36 respectively deal with?

options.A: Sections 34 to 36 apply to (i) the issue of a prospectus by a company incorporated outside India under section 389, exactly as they apply to a prospectus issued by an Indian company, and (ii) the issue of IDRs by a foreign company; section 34 deals with criminal liability for mis-statements in a prospectus, section 35 deals with civil liability for mis-statement in a prospectus, and section 36 deals with punishment for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money
options.B: Sections 34 to 36 apply only to IDR issuances and have no application whatsoever to prospectuses issued by companies incorporated outside India under section 389
options.C: Section 34 deals with civil liability, section 35 deals with criminal liability, and section 36 deals with punishment for fraudulent inducement - the reverse of the actual allocation between civil and criminal liability provisions
options.D: Sections 34 to 36 apply only where the foreign company has established a place of business in India; foreign companies issuing prospectuses or IDRs without any Indian place of business are outside the scope of section 391(1)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Sections 34 to 36 apply to (i) the issue of a prospectus by a company incorporated outside India under section 389, exactly as they apply to a prospectus issued by an Indian company, and (ii) the issue of IDRs by a foreign company; section 34 deals with criminal liability for mis-statements in a prospectus, section 35 deals with civil liability for mis-statement in a prospectus, and section 36 deals with punishment for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money

Section 391(1) extends the Indian-company prospectus liability framework - criminal liability (section 34), civil liability (section 35), and fraudulent-inducement punishment (section 36) - to both foreign-company prospectuses issued under section 389 and to IDR issuances, ensuring investor protections are not diluted merely because the issuer is incorporated outside India.

question_html: Under section 391(2), when does Chapter XX (Winding Up) apply mutatis mutandis for the closure of a foreign company's place of business in India, and subject to which other provision?

options.A: Chapter XX applies to every closure of a foreign company's place of business in India, regardless of whether it has raised any money through securities offerings and regardless of whether any such money remains unrepaid or unredeemed
options.B: Subject to the provisions of section 376 (power to wind up foreign companies although dissolved), the provisions of Chapter XX shall apply mutatis mutandis for closure of the place of business of a foreign company in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India, in case such foreign company has raised monies through offer or issue of securities under Chapter XXII which have NOT been repaid or redeemed
options.C: Chapter XX applies only where the foreign company is simultaneously being wound up in its home jurisdiction; closure of an Indian place of business alone, without a parallel home-jurisdiction winding up, is outside section 391(2)'s scope
options.D: Section 391(2) makes Chapter XX inapplicable to foreign companies altogether, on the basis that winding up of a foreign entity's Indian operations is governed exclusively by section 376 rather than by Chapter XX

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Subject to the provisions of section 376 (power to wind up foreign companies although dissolved), the provisions of Chapter XX shall apply mutatis mutandis for closure of the place of business of a foreign company in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India, in case such foreign company has raised monies through offer or issue of securities under Chapter XXII which have NOT been repaid or redeemed

Section 391(2)'s application of Chapter XX is deliberately conditional - it kicks in only where the foreign company has raised money through securities under Chapter XXII that remains unrepaid or unredeemed, and operates subject to (i.e., without displacing) section 376's separate power to wind up foreign companies even if already dissolved elsewhere.

question_html: If a foreign company contravenes the provisions of Chapter XXII, what is the fine range applicable to the foreign company itself (including for continuing contravention), and what is the fine range applicable to every officer of the foreign company who is in default?

options.A: The foreign company's fine range is Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 5,00,000, and the officer's fine range is Rs. 1,00,000 to Rs. 3,00,000 - the reverse of the actual statutory allocation between company and officer
options.B: Contravention of Chapter XXII attracts imprisonment only (with no fine component) for both the foreign company and its officers in default, for a term which may extend to 1 year
options.C: The foreign company shall be punishable with a fine of not less than Rs. 1,00,000 but which may extend to Rs. 3,00,000, and, in case of a continuing offence, with an additional fine which may extend to Rs. 50,000 for every day after the first during which the contravention continues; every officer of the foreign company who is in default shall be punishable with a fine of not less than Rs. 25,000 but which may extend to Rs. 5,00,000
options.D: There is no continuing-offence additional fine for a foreign company under section 392; the base fine range of Rs. 1,00,000 to Rs. 3,00,000 applies as a one-time penalty regardless of how long the contravention continues

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The foreign company shall be punishable with a fine of not less than Rs. 1,00,000 but which may extend to Rs. 3,00,000, and, in case of a continuing offence, with an additional fine which may extend to Rs. 50,000 for every day after the first during which the contravention continues; every officer of the foreign company who is in default shall be punishable with a fine of not less than Rs. 25,000 but which may extend to Rs. 5,00,000

Section 392 fixes the company's base fine at Rs. 1,00,000 to Rs. 3,00,000, with an additional continuing-offence fine of up to Rs. 50,000 per day after the first, while every officer in default faces a separate, higher-ceiling fine range of Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 5,00,000 - all without prejudice to the provisions of section 391.

question_html: Under section 393, does a foreign company's failure to comply with the provisions of Chapter XXII affect the validity of contracts it has entered into, or its liability to be sued? What restriction does apply while it remains non-compliant?

options.A: Non-compliance with Chapter XXII renders every contract entered into by the foreign company automatically void, and the company additionally becomes immune from being sued in respect of such contracts
options.B: Non-compliance has no legal consequence whatsoever - the non-compliant foreign company retains full and unrestricted rights to sue, claim set-off, counter-claim, and institute legal proceedings, exactly as if it were fully compliant
options.C: Non-compliance affects only contracts entered into AFTER the date of non-compliance is discovered; contracts entered into before discovery remain fully enforceable by the foreign company without any restriction
options.D: No - any failure by a company to comply with Chapter XXII provisions shall NOT affect the validity of any contract, dealing, or transaction entered into by the company, nor its liability to be sued in respect thereof; however, the company shall not be entitled to bring any suit, claim any set-off, make any counter-claim, or institute any legal proceeding in respect of any such contract, dealing, or transaction, UNTIL it has complied with the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - any failure by a company to comply with Chapter XXII provisions shall NOT affect the validity of any contract, dealing, or transaction entered into by the company, nor its liability to be sued in respect thereof; however, the company shall not be entitled to bring any suit, claim any set-off, make any counter-claim, or institute any legal proceeding in respect of any such contract, dealing, or transaction, UNTIL it has complied with the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013

Section 393 strikes a balance protecting third parties dealing with a non-compliant foreign company - contracts remain valid and the company remains suable - while denying the non-compliant company itself the offensive use of the courts (suing, set-off, counter-claim, or other legal proceedings) until it comes into compliance with the applicable provisions of the Act.

question_html: Under Rule 12 of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014, what consequence follows for a person who trades or carries on business under a name, title, or description suggesting registration as a foreign company under the Act, without actually being duly registered as such?

options.A: Such person or persons, unless duly registered as a foreign company under the Act and the Rules, shall be liable for investigation under section 210 of the Act, and action consequent upon that investigation shall be taken against that person
options.B: No specific consequence attaches under Rule 12; misuse of the 'foreign company' description is addressed only through the general penalty provisions of section 392, with no separate investigation mechanism
options.C: Such a person becomes automatically and retroactively registered as a foreign company by operation of Rule 12, curing the misdescription rather than triggering any investigation
options.D: Rule 12 subjects such a person only to a civil damages claim brought by the Registrar; no statutory investigation mechanism under section 210 is engaged by improper use of the 'foreign company' description

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Such person or persons, unless duly registered as a foreign company under the Act and the Rules, shall be liable for investigation under section 210 of the Act, and action consequent upon that investigation shall be taken against that person

Rule 12 specifically targets improper trading under a 'foreign company' description without due registration, triggering liability for investigation under section 210 (Investigation into affairs of company by Serious Fraud Investigation Office/Registrar/inspector) and consequent action - a distinct enforcement mechanism from the general section 392 penalty for registered foreign companies that contravene Chapter XXII.

question_html: Under the exemptions available in Chapter XXII, may the Central Government exempt any class of foreign companies (or companies incorporated/to be incorporated outside India) from provisions relating to the offering of securities, prospectus requirements, and incidental matters, where the activity is connected with an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC)?

options.A: No such exemption power exists under Chapter XXII; every foreign company, without exception, must comply with the full prospectus and securities-offering requirements regardless of whether the relevant activity occurs within an IFSC
options.B: Yes - the Central Government may, by notification, exempt any class of (a) foreign companies, or (b) companies incorporated or to be incorporated outside India (whether or not they have established, or when formed will or will not establish, a place of business in India), in so far as such exemption relates to the offering for subscription of securities, requirements relating to the prospectus, and all matters incidental thereto, in International Financial Services Centres set up under section 18 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005
options.C: The exemption power exists but is limited to companies that have ALREADY established a place of business in India; companies that have not yet established such a place of business are ineligible for any IFSC-related exemption
options.D: The Central Government's exemption power under this provision covers only annual return filing obligations (Form FC-4); it does not extend to securities offering, prospectus requirements, or any incidental matters

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - the Central Government may, by notification, exempt any class of (a) foreign companies, or (b) companies incorporated or to be incorporated outside India (whether or not they have established, or when formed will or will not establish, a place of business in India), in so far as such exemption relates to the offering for subscription of securities, requirements relating to the prospectus, and all matters incidental thereto, in International Financial Services Centres set up under section 18 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005

This IFSC-specific exemption power allows the Central Government to notify relief from securities-offering and prospectus-related requirements for foreign companies (or companies incorporated/to be incorporated outside India) operating in IFSCs, regardless of whether they have established, or will establish, any other place of business in India - reflecting the specialised regulatory treatment IFSCs receive under Indian law.

Before opening the Pune office, was Vantablack Solutions Pte. Ltd. already a 'foreign company' under the Companies Act, 2013, purely on account of its electronic-mode sales to Indian customers?

options.A: No - a company can never be classified as a 'foreign company' under section 2(42) without a physical branch or office located within India; electronic-mode business activity alone is categorically insufficient
options.B: No - electronic-mode business activity only brings a company within section 2(42) if its main server is physically located within India; since Vantablack Solutions Pte. Ltd.'s operations are run from outside India, it falls outside the definition
options.C: Yes - selling products through e-commerce platforms via data interchange and digital supply transactions constitutes conducting business through 'electronic mode', which counts as having a place of business in India under section 2(42); combined with the fact that it conducts business activity in India (selling to Indian customers), Vantablack Solutions Pte. Ltd. is a 'foreign company' even without any physical office, exactly as illustrated by the Search & Find Pte. Ltd. example in the study material

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - selling products through e-commerce platforms via data interchange and digital supply transactions constitutes conducting business through 'electronic mode', which counts as having a place of business in India under section 2(42); combined with the fact that it conducts business activity in India (selling to Indian customers), Vantablack Solutions Pte. Section 2(42), read with the inclusive definition of 'electronic mode' (covering B2C transactions, data interchange, and digital supply transactions regardless of where the main server is installed), squarely covers Vantablack Solutions Pte. Bayview Technologies Ltd., a company incorporated in Ireland with a place of business in India, is a subsidiary of Global Bayview Holdings Plc., its Australia-incorporated ultimate holding company, which follows a financial year running from 1st July to 30th June for consolidation purposes outside India. Bayview Technologies Ltd. is required to consolidate its own accounts with Global Bayview Holdings Plc. and wishes to align its own financial year accordingly, instead of following the default 31st March year-end.

Assuming Bayview Technologies Ltd. is permitted to follow the 1st July to 30th June financial year, within what period after the close of that financial year must it deliver its financial statement (together with the related party transactions, profit repatriation, and fund transfer statements) to the Registrar, and by how much may this period be extended?

options.A: Within 60 days of the close of the financial year, matching the annual return (Form FC-4) timeline, with no provision for any extension of this period under any circumstance
options.B: Within 30 days of the close of the financial year, matching the timeline for reporting alterations to previously delivered documents under Form FC-2
options.C: Within 6 months of the close of the financial year (i.e., ordinarily by 31st December, if its financial year ends 30th June); the Registrar may, for any special reason, and on a written application, extend this period by a period not exceeding 3 months
options.D: Within 12 months of the close of the financial year, with the Central Government (rather than the Registrar) empowered to grant an unlimited further extension upon application

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Within 6 months of the close of the financial year (i.e., ordinarily by 31st December, if its financial year ends 30th June); the Registrar may, for any special reason, and on a written application, extend this period by a period not exceeding 3 months

Regardless of which 12-month period constitutes its financial year, the 6-month filing window (extendable by up to 3 further months by the Registrar, for special reason, on written application) applies uniformly to the financial statement and the three additional statements (related party transactions, repatriation of profits, transfer of funds) required under Rule 4.

Since Alderney Resources Ltd.'s prospectus is being issued more than 2 years after the date it became entitled to commence business, which particulars under section 387(1)(a) are exempted, and which requirements continue to apply regardless?

options.A: All particulars under section 387(1)(a), including the date and country of incorporation, are exempted once the prospectus is issued more than 2 years after the company became entitled to commence business, leaving only the section 26 matters to be stated
options.B: No particulars are exempted at all; the 2-year proviso applies only to prospectuses issued by companies that have already established a place of business in India, which Alderney Resources Ltd. has not
options.C: The exemption applies only if the prospectus is issued LESS than 2 years after the company became entitled to commence business, so Alderney Resources Ltd. (with more than 10 years elapsed) does not qualify for any exemption
options.D: The particulars relating to (1) the instrument constituting/defining the company's constitution, (2) the enactments/provisions under which incorporation was effected, and (3) the Indian inspection address for those instruments/enactments are exempted under the proviso to section 387(1); however, the prospectus must still be dated and signed, must still disclose the date and country of incorporation and whether a place of business has been established in India (and if so, its address), and must still state the matters specified under section 26

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The particulars relating to (1) the instrument constituting/defining the company's constitution, (2) the enactments/provisions under which incorporation was effected, and (3) the Indian inspection address for those instruments/enactments are exempted under the proviso to section 387(1); however, the prospectus must still be dated and signed, must still disclose the date and country of incorporation and whether a place of business has been established in India (and if so, its address), and must still state the matters specified under section 26

Given that the prospectus includes a valuation statement purporting to be made by an independent property valuation expert, what must Alderney Resources Ltd. ensure under section 388 before the prospectus can lawfully be issued?

options.D: Section 388 applies only to statements made by legal experts (such as solicitors), not to statements made by property valuation experts, so no consent is required for this particular statement

Correct answer: (A) The valuation expert must have given, and must not have withdrawn before delivery of the prospectus for registration, his written consent to the issue of the prospectus with his statement included in the form and context in which it is included; alternatively, the prospectus must itself state that he has given and has not withdrawn such consent

Section 388's expert-consent requirement is entirely independent of the section 387(1) proviso's 2-year timing exemption (which concerns only certain constitutional-document particulars) - since the prospectus includes a valuation expert's statement, that expert's written, unwithdrawn consent (obtained before delivery of the prospectus for registration) remains a mandatory precondition to lawful issuance.

Separately and unrelated to Solingen Materials AG, Craterhill Mining Ltd., incorporated in Canada (with no place of business in India), proposes to merge into an Indian company registered under the Companies Act, 2013, with the scheme of merger providing for shareholders of Craterhill Mining Ltd. to receive consideration partly in cash and partly in Depository Receipts.

Does the fact that Solingen Materials AG has no place of business in India prevent it from issuing Indian Depository Receipts?

options.A: Yes - Rule 13 expressly requires a foreign company to have already established a place of business in India before it can issue any IDRs, making Solingen Materials AG ineligible until it opens an Indian office
options.B: Yes - IDR issuance is available only to companies that already comply with section 379(2)'s 50%-Indian-holding threshold, which necessarily presupposes an established place of business in India
options.C: No - under Rule 13 of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014, no company incorporated or to be incorporated outside India, WHETHER OR NOT it has established (or may or may not establish) any place of business in India, shall make an issue of IDRs unless it complies with the conditions mentioned in Rule 13, in addition to the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2009 and any RBI directions - so the absence of an Indian place of business does not, by itself, bar Solingen Materials AG from issuing IDRs
options.D: The eligibility to issue IDRs depends solely on whether Solingen Materials AG's home-country (German) securities regulator has separately approved the issuance, with Rule 13's conditions being inapplicable to companies without an Indian place of business

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - under Rule 13 of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014, no company incorporated or to be incorporated outside India, WHETHER OR NOT it has established (or may or may not establish) any place of business in India, shall make an issue of IDRs unless it complies with the conditions mentioned in Rule 13, in addition to the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2009 and any RBI directions - so the absence of an Indian place of business does not, by itself, bar Solingen Materials AG from issuing IDRs

Rule 13 is explicit that IDR issuance is open to a company incorporated (or to be incorporated) outside India regardless of whether it has, or will, establish any place of business in India - subject instead to compliance with Rule 13's own conditions, the SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2009, and any RBI directions.

options.D: Craterhill Mining Ltd.'s status depends on whether Canada is a jurisdiction notified by the Central Government for Chapter XV merger purposes, a factual question that, once resolved either way, has no bearing on whether it is a 'foreign company' under section 234(2)
